summary: Summarizes the issues in the relationship between the IETF and the Internet Society, as discussed by the Poised working group, in order to gauge consensus. It was replaced by RFC 8712.

plainLanguage.summary: Two groups work together, and this note lists the questions about how they should team up so people can talk it over.

questions: what is the relationship between ietf and isoc
subtitle: Defining the division of responsibilities between the IETF and the Internet Society.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, the IETF needed help with legal and organizational issues, but the relationship with the Internet Society (ISOC) needed clear boundaries to preserve IETF's technical independence.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC summarizes the Poised Working Group's recommendations: the IETF remains responsible for technical standards and quality, while ISOC provides legal protection, facilitates non-technical processes, and assists with appeals, but has no influence on technical content.
tldr.outcome: This agreement was replaced by RFC 8712 as governance evolved, but it established the foundational principle that IETF maintains technical independence.

today: RFC 2031 is obsolete and replaced by RFC 8712. However, it documents the foundational principle that has guided the IETF-ISOC relationship: the IETF maintains technical independence while ISOC provides organizational and legal support.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) develops and maintains Internet Standards through volunteers and working groups. As the Internet grew, the IETF faced increasing non-technical issues: legal problems, licensing, disputes, and organizational structure. The Poised Working Group recommended moving these issues to the Internet Society (ISOC), a related organization.

However, moving responsibilities required clear boundaries. The IETF participants and ISOC board needed to understand exactly which organization was responsible for what, to prevent non-technical concerns from interfering with technical work and preserve the IETF's technical independence.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF makes the technical decisions about how the Internet works. ISOC is another group that can help with legal and boring administrative stuff. This document says which group does what.

sections.title: The Division of Responsibilities
sections.content:
The boundary condition is clear: the IETF remains responsible for developing and ensuring the quality of Internet Standards. ISOC has no influence whatsoever on the technical content of standards.

ISOC provides a legal umbrella, including legal insurance for IETF officers, legal protection of the RFC series so documents can be freely distributed but not altered, and protection against intellectual property disputes. ISOC also assists the standards process by appointing the Nominations Committee chair, approving IAB candidates, and reviewing documents that describe the standards process.
sections.plainLanguage: IETF decides what the Internet standards are. ISOC handles the lawyers and protects IETF's documents from being stolen or changed.

sections.title: Risks and Alternatives
sections.content:
Moving responsibilities to ISOC creates some risk: the IETF no longer has absolute control over all decisions. However, the RFC argues this is an opportunity, not a threat. The alternatives were worse: ignoring growth would risk making IETF insignificant or drowning it in lawsuits; the IETF handling everything itself would distract from technical work.

The relationship works because ISOC, like the IETF, uses public discussion and consensus building, and puts Internet-related work up for IETF discussion rather than deciding unilaterally.
sections.plainLanguage: By letting ISOC handle the boring stuff, IETF engineers can focus on what they do best: working on the standards. ISOC is trustworthy because they use the same consensus approach.
